anchor_text: doth the melted snow Upon the valleys, whose low vassal seat The Alps doth spit and void his rheum upon
summary: King Charles tells his nobles to rush on Henry's army as meltwater from the Alps crashes down onto the valleys below, which sit as 'vassal seats' — low, subordinate positions — while the mountains above them 'spit and void their rheum' (discharge their phlegm, their runoff) upon them. anchor_text: in our marches through the country, there be nothing compell'd from the villages, nothing taken but paid for

anchor_text: You know me by my habit

anchor_text: 'Tis a hooded valour; and when it appears, it will bate
summary: The Constable is mocking the Dauphin's alleged courage by comparing it to a hooded falcon. A falconer keeps a hawk 'hooded' — a leather cap over its head — to keep it calm and manageable; when the hood comes off, the bird beats its wings restlessly ('bates'), straining to escape. The Constable's point: the Dauphin's bravery exists only under the hood of ignorance; the moment it is exposed to real battle, it will panic and bolt.

'Bate' (also spelled 'bait') means the violent, frantic flapping of a hawk's wings when it tries to fly from the fist before being allowed. It was a sign of an untrained or frightened bird. The Constable's insult is precise: the Dauphin's courage is kept artificially calm by never being tested; once tested, it will 'bate' — flap, panic, and be lost.

anchor_text: That island of England breeds very valiant creatures. Their mastiffs are of unmatchable courage
summary: The English mastiff was famous across Europe as the fiercest and most powerful breed of dog, praised by foreign visitors and used in the bear- and bull-baiting arenas that were prominent London entertainments. Rambures' comment that England's very dogs are courageous is a back-handed compliment meant to demean English soldiers as mere brutes — brave but without the wit to recognise danger.

Orleans's reply — that the mastiffs run 'winking' (with eyes shut) into a Russian bear's mouth — converts Rambures' inadvertent praise into pure mockery: English courage is blind animal recklessness, not strategic valor. The Russian bear (a byword for savage size) was a stock figure of the period.

anchor_text: give them great meals of beef and iron and steel, they will eat like wolves and fight like devils
summary: The Constable invokes the Elizabethan stereotype of English soldiers as heavy beef-eaters: beef was the staple of the English diet, and the English were mocked — and feared — across Europe for the ferocity it supposedly gave them. The dark joke is that the depleted English army, which historically marched hungry and sick to Agincourt, has lost the one advantage the French concede it. anchor_text: Like sacrifices, by their watchful fires
summary: The Chorus compares the English soldiers sitting quietly by their fires to animals waiting to be sacrificed — an image from ancient religious ritual where a beast is kept calm before slaughter. It calls attention to how helpless and doomed the English appear, making their eventual victory all the more extraordinary.

Animals slated for sacrifice were meant to go willingly and in silence, which overlaid the image of the 'patiently' waiting soldiers with a sense of chosen doom and religious solemnity. anchor_text: Upon his royal face there is no note

anchor_text: A largess universal like the sun

anchor_text: There is some soul of goodness in things evil
summary: Henry opens with a paradox: even bad things, if studied carefully, can teach something good. He works through the logic: the threat of the French army ('our bad neighbour') makes the English rise early, which is healthy, teaches them to be ready for death, and — as he puts it — lets a man 'gather honey from the weed.' The speech is a brief formal argument building from a general maxim to concrete application.

'Good husbandry' means careful household or estate management — prudence and thrift. 'Outward consciences' casts the enemy as a kind of external moral voice reminding the soldiers to prepare their souls. 'Make a moral of the devil himself' means extract a lesson even from evil. The speech sets up Henry as a king who thinks his way through danger rather than simply showing courage.

Fluellen's point (no talking in camp before battle) is technically correct, and the scene's comedy is that the pedantic Welshman is right.

anchor_text: wars of Pompey the Great

anchor_text: The violet smells to him as it doth to me

anchor_text: roaring devil i' the old play, that every one may pare his nails with a wooden dagger
summary: The Boy is comparing Pistol to a stock comic villain from the older morality plays of the previous century: the Devil, who appeared on stage roaring and waving a wooden dagger, so obviously harmless that any bystander could approach and trim his claws with it. By Shakespeare's time the morality tradition was dated and associated with unsophisticated popular entertainment, so calling Pistol a 'roaring devil i' the old play' doubly belittles him: he is a cheap theatrical fraud AND a figure already out of fashion. The detail that 'every one may pare his nails with a wooden dagger' intensifies the mockery — the devil is so toothless that his only weapon can be borrowed as a nail-file. anchor_text: Disorder, that hath spoil'd us, friend us now
summary: The Constable turns the cause of the French defeat into a desperate rallying cry: the very chaos ('disorder') that destroyed their formation should now be their weapon. The logic is paradoxical — they have nothing left to lose, so instead of fighting as an army they should throw themselves into the English mass as a mob and perhaps smother them by sheer weight of numbers.

The Constable's next line, 'Let us on heaps go offer up our lives' (2281), makes the strategy explicit: abandon military order entirely and become a human avalanche. The irony is sharp given the French commanders' pre-battle contempt for the ragged English ('disordered' in appearance): the proud French army, which prided itself on chivalric formations, is now reduced to begging disorder to save it. Editors compare this to the rhetorical figure of paradiastole, the redescription of a vice as a virtue (here disorder recast as a potential ally). Cf. Oxford Shakespeare, Henry V, ed. Apostrophe is the correct primary device; the secondary label 'paradiastole' in the detail is a slight stretch (the Constable petitions disorder rather than rebranding it as a virtue), but the core irony reading — that the cause of defeat is now invoked as saviour — is mainstream and the annotation's headline gloss does not assert paradiastole, so the over-labelling is confined to the detail and does not constitute a refutable misreading.

anchor_text: Larding the plain
summary: 'Larding' comes from the cooking term for threading strips of fat through lean meat to keep it moist; here Exeter uses it as a grim metaphor — York's blood richly soaks and 'bastes' the ground. The word turns the battlefield earth into something that has received the slain duke's body, and all its blood, as an offering.
detail: The OED records 'lard' (v.) in the figurative sense of 'to enrich or cover the surface of' from the sixteenth century. Shakespeare uses the cooking register deliberately: it captures the grotesque physicality of a body drenched in blood while also, paradoxically, conferring a kind of richness or value on the dead — the plain has been given something precious. Exeter's eulogy throughout this speech works by pulling the horror of battlefield death into formal, almost ceremonial language.

The cooking-register reading of 'lard' (to baste/enrich with fat, transferred to blood) is mainstream, well-attested in OED and Onions, and the claim that Exeter's diction works ceremonially is confirmed by the surrounding speech (insteeped, espous'd, seal'd).

anchor_text: espous'd to death, with blood he seal'd A testament
summary: Exeter stacks three legal and ceremonial terms — 'espous'd' (married), 'seal'd' (authenticated a document with a wax seal), and 'testament' (a legal will) — to describe York dying in Suffolk's arms. The effect is to re-describe a battlefield death as a solemn marriage contract, with blood instead of a wax seal. York has formally bound himself to his dead kinsman, as spouses are bound to each other.
detail: The metaphor draws on two overlapping Elizabethan legal ceremonies. Marriage ('espousals') required a public pledge and a joining of hands; a legal deed or will required the maker's seal pressed in wax. Both were solemn, witnessed acts with permanent consequences. By wedding the two images, Shakespeare turns York's dying embrace of Suffolk's body into a document that cannot be revoked — 'noble-ending love' ratified by the only medium available on a battlefield. The compressed legalism is characteristic of Shakespeare's late-history style, where high emotion is given formal, almost contractual dignity.

anchor_text: all my mother came into mine eyes And gave me up to tears
summary: Exeter does not mean his actual mother. 'The mother' was an Elizabethan medical term for a powerful suffocating emotion, sometimes called hysterica passio, thought to rise from the womb (Latin matrix, 'mother') and cause uncontrollable weeping or choking — even in men. Exeter is saying that his feminine, emotional side overwhelmed his soldierly self-control.

Shakespeare uses the same term in King Lear (2.4): 'O, how this mother swells up toward my heart! / Hysterica passio, down, thou climbing sorrow.' Exeter's apology — 'I had not so much of man in me' — confirms that he reads his tears as an incursion of the feminine into the masculine armour of a soldier.

'All my mother' as the Elizabethan medical concept of hysterica passio is the standard editorial reading, supported by the direct King Lear parallel ('O, how this mother swells up toward my heart! / Hysterica passio'), and the line's immediate gloss ('I had not so much of man in me') confirms the feminized-emotion interpretation in the text itself.

anchor_text: Then every soldier kill his prisoners
summary: Hearing a fresh French alarm, Henry orders every English soldier to execute his French prisoners immediately. The order was controversial even in Shakespeare's day: Holinshed records it as a real command at Agincourt and explains it as a military necessity — the English feared that thousands of prisoners at their backs would re-arm and attack if a renewed French assault succeeded. The play justifies it twice: here by the new alarum, and in 4.7 by the French slaughter of the unarmed boys guarding the English baggage.
detail: Holinshed (Chronicles, 1587) describes the order and the reluctance of some soldiers to carry it out, since killing prisoners meant forfeiting their ransoms — substantial financial stakes. The laws of medieval warfare permitted killing prisoners whose escape or re-arming posed a genuine threat, but killing prisoners who had already surrendered was otherwise dishonourable. Shakespeare's double motivation — the French advance and the boys' massacre — may be a deliberate effort to make the command defensible to his audience. Fluellen's reaction in 4.7 ('Kill the poys and the luggage! 'tis expressly against the law of arms') shows that the legality was not taken for granted. The order is one of the play's most debated moments in modern performance and criticism.

The interpretation that Henry's order is triggered by the new alarum in this scene and that the play provides a second justification in 4.7 (the boys' massacre) is accurate; the note that this double motivation may be a deliberate authorial choice to render the command more defensible is a mainstream critical observation, not an overreach.

anchor_text: Kill the poys and the luggage
summary: Fluellen is outraged that the French have attacked and killed the English boys left to guard the baggage train ('the luggage') — a serious violation of the recognized laws of war. 'Poys' is Fluellen's Welsh-accented pronunciation of 'boys.' Holinshed's Chronicles records that during the actual battle of Agincourt French raiders attacked the English baggage camp, where the unarmed servants and boys were stationed, and Henry's order to kill the French prisoners followed in part from this.
detail: The 'laws of arms' (chivalric and military law, codified in treatises such as Honoré Bouvet's Arbre des Batailles, c. 1387, and Christine de Pizan's Faits d'Armes) stipulated that non-combatants, prisoners, and unresisting men were not to be slaughtered. Attacking the luggage — and killing the boys with it — violates those norms. The play uses the incident to give Henry's brutal prisoner-killing order (mentioned in 4.6 and reiterated here) a defensive justification. Holinshed, however, places the events in uncertain chronological relation; modern historians debate whether the baggage raid or the threat of a renewed French cavalry charge was the primary cause of the order.

sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles of England, Scotland, and Ireland (1587), on the Battle of Agincourt, 25 October 1415, and the attack on the English baggage train.

The reading that this is a laws-of-war violation, that 'poys' reflects Fluellen's Welsh accent, and that Holinshed records the baggage-train attack are all mainstream-defensible; the annotation correctly notes the historiographical debate about the chronological order of the baggage raid versus the prisoner-killing order.

anchor_text: he was porn at Monmouth
summary: Fluellen's Welsh accent converts every English 'b' into 'p': 'porn' = born, 'poys' = boys, 'prains' = brains, 'pattle' = battle. This is consistent throughout the scene and is Shakespeare's theatrical shorthand for a Welsh accent. Henry V was indeed born at Monmouth in Wales in 1387, making him a countryman of Fluellen — a point the scene exploits comically and warmly.

anchor_text: Alexander the Pig was born
summary: Fluellen means 'Alexander the Great' — 'Pig' is his Welsh-accented 'Big' (just as 'b' becomes 'p' throughout). He then comically defends the title: 'is not pig great? The pig, or the great, or the mighty, or the huge, or the magnanimous, are all one reckonings.' Alexander the Great (356-323 BCE), king of Macedon, was the ancient world's supreme military conqueror, subjugating the Persian Empire, Egypt, and reaching into India. Fluellen wants to compare him to Henry V.

Fluellen's comparison — Macedon and Monmouth both have rivers, therefore the two kings are alike — parodies humanist methods of finding 'figures' (typological or analogical patterns) in history. The absurdity of arguing from a shared river heightens the comedy while the underlying comparison (a great king at war) is genuinely meant.

The phonological explanation ('Pig' = 'Big' via Welsh b-to-p shift) is sound, supported by Fluellen's own subsequent defence ('is not pig great?'), and the description of Alexander's significance and the Plutarch-North source is mainstream-defensible; the parody of humanist typological method is a recognised reading without overreach.

anchor_text: there is figures in all things. Alexander, God knows
summary: Fluellen claims that history contains 'figures' — analogies or typological patterns linking one great person to another. He then lands on the comparison's dark pivot: Alexander, 'being a little intoxicates in his prains,' killed his best friend Cleitus. Cleitus the Black was one of Alexander's most loyal generals, who saved his life at the Battle of the Granicus; Alexander stabbed him during a drunken quarrel in 328 BCE when Cleitus praised Philip II over his son. Fluellen is about to argue that Henry's rejection of Falstaff was similar — but milder, since Henry was sober.
detail: Plutarch's Life of Alexander (North 1579), ch. 50-51, gives the full account of the killing of Cleitus: a drunken banquet, Cleitus praising Philip and mocking Alexander's claim to divine birth, Alexander hurling a spear through him, then overnight remorse. The episode was notorious as a blot on Alexander's greatness. Fluellen's 'figures in all things' echoes Renaissance typological reading of history, whereby ancient events were understood to prefigure or parallel later ones.

anchor_text: turn'd away the fat knight with the great belly doublet
summary: Fluellen draws his parallel: as the drunken Alexander killed his old friend Cleitus, so the clear-headed Henry 'turned away' (rejected) his old companion Sir John Falstaff — the 'fat knight with the great belly doublet.' Fluellen has forgotten Falstaff's name, and Gower has to supply it. The rejection occurred at the end of Henry IV Part 2 (5.5), when the newly crowned Henry publicly disavows Falstaff before a crowd. A 'doublet' was a close-fitted jacket; a 'great belly doublet' is one stretched out by an enormous paunch.

He rates Henry higher than Alexander by noting that Henry rejected (not killed) his friend, and did it 'in his right wits and his good judgements' — sober, deliberate, just — whereas Alexander killed in drink and rage. The comedy of his forgetting Falstaff's name and having to ask Gower undercuts the solemnity: the most famous figure of the tetralogy is unnamed in his final mention in the cycle. Gipes (TLN 2365) means jibes or taunts.

anchor_text: I have fin'd these bones of mine for ransom
summary: Henry means he has already 'fined' (settled, fixed, pledged) his person — literally 'these bones' — against being held for ransom. Before the battle, when Montjoy had brought the first French demand that Henry pay ransom to avoid destruction, Henry refused, saying his body was all he had to pledge. Now, after the English victory, he greets the herald's return with bitter irony: 'Have you come again for ransom? I already wagered my bones on this fight.' 'To fine' here means to put an end to the matter by pledging, from Latin finire.

anchor_text: wander o'er this bloody field To book our dead, and then to bury them
summary: Montjoy asks permission to walk the battlefield and 'book' (count and record in writing) the French dead before burying them. 'To book' = to register in a list or account. After a medieval battle, heralds and clerks moved through the field recording the dead by name and rank, both to notify families and to establish the legal questions of ransom, inheritance, and honours. Sorting 'nobles from common men' was especially important because noble corpses commanded ransoms and required separate burial rites.

anchor_text: Fret fetlock deep in gore, and with wild rage Yerk out their armed heels
summary: Montjoy describes wounded warhorses standing in blood up to their fetlocks, kicking out their heels at their dead masters. The 'fetlock' is the tuft of hair and joint just above the horse's hoof. 'Fret' means to chafe or wear against. 'Yerk' (also 'jerk') means to kick or lash out suddenly. The image is vivid and grim: the horses, maddened by wounds, are accidentally trampling the very men who rode them — 'killing them twice.'

summary: Henry formally names the battlefield 'Agincourt' (the castle nearby gives the field its name) and fixes it to the feast day of Saints Crispin and Crispinian — 25 October. Both Crispin and his twin Crispinian are named: 'Crispianus' is the Latinate form of Crispinian. The St. Crispin's Day speech in the scene before this one (4.3) already made the feast day the centerpiece of Henry's rallying of his troops. The battle of Agincourt was fought on that date in 1415.

anchor_text: your great-uncle Edward the Plack Prince of Wales
summary: Fluellen reminds Henry that his ancestors — Henry's grandfather Edward III and his great-uncle the Black Prince — fought a great battle in France in the same region. Fluellen has read 'in the chronicles' about it, meaning Holinshed. 'Plack' is Fluellen's pronunciation of 'Black.' The Black Prince (Edward of Woodstock, 1330-1376) was the eldest son of Edward III, Prince of Wales, and the greatest English warrior of his generation. The battle Fluellen alludes to is Crécy (1346) or possibly Poitiers (1356).
detail: The Black Prince is so called from his black armour. He won the famous English victory at Poitiers (1356), capturing the French King John II — a precedent that shadows Agincourt. He died before his father Edward III and so never became king; his son became Richard II. Henry V is the Black Prince's great-nephew (not grandson), though Fluellen says 'your grandfather... and your great-uncle': Henry's grandfather was John of Gaunt, son of Edward III, and the Black Prince was Gaunt's elder brother — hence Henry's great-uncle.

The genealogical identification is correct (the Black Prince was Henry V's great-uncle, not grandfather; the text has Fluellen say 'your grandfather... and your great-uncle' covering both Edward III and the Black Prince), the annotation accurately tracks the distinction; the association of the region with Crécy and Poitiers is supported by Holinshed and the play's own allusion.

anchor_text: 'tis the gage of one that I should fight withal
summary: A 'gage' is a pledge — typically a glove or gauntlet — thrown down to challenge an opponent to combat. Picking it up means accepting the challenge; the challenger must wear the gage until the fight is settled. Williams exchanged gloves with the disguised Henry the night before the battle (4.1) as a pledge to fight after the battle was won. 'Withal' is an archaic form meaning 'with' (used at the end of a phrase). Williams wears his opponent's glove in his cap as the visible mark of the pledge.

summary: Henry tells Fluellen that the glove he is giving him was taken in single combat from the Duke of Alencon during the battle. 'Down together' means they were in close, grappling combat, both fallen. John I, Duke of Alencon (d. 1415), was a French commander at Agincourt who, according to some accounts, came close enough to Henry to strike off a piece of the king's crown during hand-to-hand fighting before being killed. The glove as a token from his helm (helmet) is Henry's invention: he is now giving Fluellen a booby trap — William's matching glove — dressed up as a war trophy.

The comic plot hinges on Henry giving Fluellen the glove Williams carries as his challenge-pledge, virtually guaranteeing Williams will strike Fluellen when he sees it in his cap — and Henry reveals the trick in his aside (TLN 2479-2489), sending Warwick and Gloucester to prevent any real harm.

anchor_text: Fluellen valiant And, touch'd with choler, hot as gunpowder
summary: 'Choler' (also spelled 'choler' or 'cholera') was one of the four bodily humours in the medical theory inherited from ancient Greece and still current in Shakespeare's day. The choleric humour — yellow bile — was associated with quick temper, aggression, and passionate anger. A person 'touch'd with choler' is short-fused and prone to violent reaction. Henry is predicting, accurately, that if Williams strikes Fluellen (who is wearing Williams's challenge-glove), the proud Welshman's choleric temperament will flare up into open violence rather than any diplomatic backing-down.

'Hot as gunpowder' turns the medical metaphor into a vivid simile: Fluellen will not just flare up but explode. Gunpowder was still a relatively new and spectacular military technology, making the comparison feel modern and apt.

anchor_text: 'Sblood! an arrant traitor as any is in the universal
summary: 'Sblood' is a contracted oath — 'by God's blood' — one of the common Elizabethan profanities invoking Christ's wounds or body. Fluellen uses it in genuine fury when Williams strikes him over the glove.

The 1606 Act to Restrain Abuses of Players forbade such oaths on the stage, and later quartos and folios often mute or bowdlerize them; that the First Folio text of Henry V retains it here signals the vigor of Fluellen's outburst.

anchor_text: give treason his payment into plows, I warrant you
summary: Fluellen means to give treason its full payment — to the hilt, thoroughly. 'Into plows' is Fluellen's garbled version of 'to the plows,' a phrase meaning 'utterly' or 'straight through'; the exact idiom is muddled by his Welsh English, and editors have proposed various emendations. The sense is simply: he will punish this treachery completely.
detail: The phrase 'give ... his payment into plows' resists a single clean gloss. Some editors read 'plows' as 'blows' misheard or misspelled; others take it as a comic extension of 'payment' meaning execution or punishment. Fluellen's speech throughout the play combines genuine military honor with phonologically distorted English ('p' for 'b' is his most marked feature: 'prawls' for 'brawls', 'prabbles' for 'brabbles', 'pashful' for 'bashful'). The audience is meant to catch the fury beneath the malapropism.

anchor_text: It was ourself thou didst abuse
summary: Henry reveals that he himself was the 'common man' Williams argued with the night before Agincourt, walking in disguise among the troops as 'Harry le Roy.' The word 'ourself' is the royal plural — a king speaking as the embodiment of the state — making the revelation more than personal: Williams unknowingly quarreled with the office of the crown itself.
detail: The royal plural ('we,' 'ourself,' 'us' for a single king) was standard formal usage throughout the medieval and early modern period, grounded in the doctrine of the king's two bodies: the king's person is inseparable from the body politic, so he speaks as 'we.' Henry's use of it precisely here — identifying the disguised common man with 'ourself' — dramatizes the gap Williams has transgressed. Williams's defense, that the king appeared as a 'common man,' is legally and morally sound: he could not have committed the crime of disrespecting majesty because majesty was deliberately hidden. Henry concedes the point and rewards rather than punishes him.

anchor_text: the fellow has mettle enough in his belly

anchor_text: prawls, and prabbles, and quarrels, and dissensions
summary: 'Brawls' and 'brabbles' (petty quarrels) are the words Fluellen means; his Welsh accent converts 'b' to 'p' throughout the play, giving 'prawls' and 'prabbles.' anchor_text: This note doth tell me of ten thousand French
summary: The casualty count Henry reads from the herald's paper is drawn from the chronicles of Agincourt (25 October 1415). Modern estimates put French dead at around 6,000-10,000; English dead at fewer than 100. Shakespeare preserves the lopsided proportion — a tiny English force destroying the flower of French chivalry — which contemporaries read as proof of divine favor.
detail: Holinshed's Chronicles (1587) give a French death toll of about 10,000, with a sharply stratified breakdown by rank that Shakespeare follows almost exactly: princes, barons, and knights far outnumbering common soldiers. Henry lists the names of the chief French dead (TLN 2574-2582) — Constable d'Albret, the Admiral of France, Lord Rambures, Alencon, Brabant, Bar, and several earls — most of whom are characters already named in the play. That '500 were but yesterday dubbed knights' is also in Holinshed, stressing that France had just promoted men it expected to be victorious. The contrast with the English dead — only 'five and twenty' common soldiers plus York and Suffolk — is the scene's theological crux: the numbers are so extreme that Henry treats them as beyond military explanation.

anchor_text: Edward the Duke of York, the Earl of Suffolk, Sir Richard Ketly, Davy Gam, esquire; None else of name
summary: The English dead of note are four: the Duke of York (cousin to the king, who begged to lead the vanguard); the Earl of Suffolk; Sir Richard Ketly; and Davy Gam, a Welsh knight knighted on the battlefield moments before he died. 'None else of name' means no one else of noble rank — the rest of the twenty-five are unnamed common soldiers.
detail: The historical Edward, Duke of York, led the English vanguard at Agincourt and was indeed killed, probably crushed in the press of battle rather than slain by a weapon. His death at 4.6 (where Exeter movingly describes York and Suffolk dying embraced) gives the English losses a face and an emotion. Davy Gam (David ap Llewelyn, known as 'Gam,' meaning 'squinting') was a Welsh soldier; Holinshed and later tradition credit him with being knighted as he lay dying on the field. Including him here, alongside great lords, is one of the play's signals that Agincourt leveled ranks — the same theme as the St. Crispin's Day speech. 'Esquire' was the rank just below knight, so listing Davy Gam last and with his given rank, not a knighthood, may reflect a slightly different tradition from the deathbed-knighting story.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on English casualties at Agincourt: the Duke of York, the Earl of Suffolk, and Davy Gam among the principal dead.

The historical identifications match Holinshed and the play; the tension between the text listing Davy Gam as 'esquire' and the tradition of his battlefield knighting is honestly flagged rather than smoothed over.

anchor_text: O God, thy arm was here; And not to us, but to thy arm alone, Ascribe we all
summary: Henry's attribution of the victory entirely to God echoes the Old Testament tradition of holy war in which God's 'arm' or 'hand' (not human strategy) wins the battle. The phrase 'God's arm' appears throughout the Psalms and prophetic books for divine military power on Israel's behalf. Henry refuses any human credit and makes it a capital offense to boast of the victory.
detail: The specific idiom 'thy arm' draws on passages such as Psalm 44:3 ('For they got not the land in possession by their own sword, neither did their own arm save them: but thy right hand, and thine arm, and the light of thy countenance') and Isaiah 59:16 ('his arm brought salvation'). Henry's speech frames Agincourt as a miracle of providential intervention — the 'plain shock and even play of battle' (a fair, straightforward fight with no stratagem) makes the outcome inexplicable by tactical means alone. His subsequent order that 'it be death' to boast of the victory, and the command to sing the hymns of thanksgiving (Non nobis and Te Deum), are the formal acts completing that theological interpretation.

anchor_text: go we in procession to the village; And be it death proclaimed through our host To boast of this
summary: Henry bans boasting of the victory on pain of death and orders a religious procession — both acts that deflect the credit from human achievement to divine favor. Holinshed confirms that the historical Henry V did issue such an order and that a solemn Te Deum was sung on the field at Agincourt.

The 'procession to the village' — presumably the nearby village of Agincourt itself — was the assembled army marching in order to give communal thanks rather than celebrating in a disorganized rout. The combination of the formal procession, the death penalty for pride, and the two prescribed hymns (Non nobis and Te Deum) constructs the aftermath of battle as a liturgical event rather than a military celebration.

anchor_text: Non nobis and Te Deum
summary: 'Non nobis' ('Not unto us') is the opening of Psalm 115, a psalm of thanksgiving that denies human pride and credits God alone: 'Non nobis, Domine, sed nomini tuo da gloriam' — 'Not to us, Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory.' The 'Te Deum' is a great ancient Christian hymn of praise beginning 'We praise thee, O God.' Together they were the liturgical formula for giving thanks after military victory. Henry orders both sung before the army marches to Calais.
detail: Psalm 115 (numbered 113 in the Latin Vulgate) was sung in the medieval military church specifically after victories, making Henry's order historically specific and not merely pious decoration. The Te Deum ('Ambrosian Hymn'), used at Matins and on great occasions of thanksgiving, was the most solemn communal act of praise available. Singing both immediately after reading the casualty lists — and immediately after banning personal boasting — translates the statistical miracle of Agincourt into a public act of worship. Holinshed confirms both hymns were sung on the field. Audiences of 1599, familiar with the Te Deum from Sunday services in the Church of England's Book of Common Prayer (where it appears at Morning Prayer), would recognize the gravity of the moment.

anchor_text: senators of the antique Rome, With the plebeians swarming at their heels, Go forth and fetch their conquering Caesar in
summary: The Chorus compares Henry's triumphal return to London to a Roman general's triumph: London's mayor and aldermen are cast as senators, the crowd as plebeians, and Henry as a conquering Caesar. This was the highest honour the Roman Republic or Empire could offer a victorious general.
detail: The Roman triumph was a formal procession voted by the Senate to a commander after a decisive victory over foreign enemies. Plutarch and Suetonius describe Caesar's triumphs in vivid detail; the senators marching out to escort the conquering general was the ritual's climax. Shakespeare uses the comparison carefully: Henry is the 'Caesar' who returns victorious, yet unlike Julius Caesar he refuses the attendant glory, forbidding the display of his battered helmet and sword ('Giving full trophy, signal, and ostent / Quite from himself to God,' lines 2630-31). The compliment is magnified by the self-erasure.

sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Caesar, in Sir Thomas North, The Lives of the Noble Grecians and Romans (1579), on Caesar's triumphs in Rome.

anchor_text: the general of our gracious empress, As in good time he may, from Ireland coming, Bringing rebellion broached on his sword
summary: This is the most precisely datable line Shakespeare ever wrote. The 'general of our gracious empress' almost certainly refers to Robert Devereux, Earl of Essex, whom Queen Elizabeth sent to Ireland in March 1599 to suppress Tyrone's rebellion. Shakespeare imagines Essex returning victorious with 'rebellion broached on his sword' — rebellion spitted like meat on a skewer. Essex left London to huge crowds but returned in September 1599 without victory, having made an unauthorised truce. This Chorus was therefore written between March and September 1599.
detail: Essex's Irish campaign was the defining political event of that summer: he commanded a large army and had the Queen's trust and the city's enthusiasm. The comparison is framed as a hypothetical ('As, by a lower but loving likelihood, / Were now the general') — a lower parallel to Henry's grander return, not a direct equation. The word 'broached' means to spit on a broach (a spit for roasting), a vivid image for rebellion skewered and defeated. Essex's failure to achieve that outcome, and his unauthorised return to court and house arrest, make this passage a moment of extraordinary topical poignancy if the play was performed after September 1599. The allusion dates Henry V to 1599, the same year as Julius Caesar and As You Like It, and is one of the strongest internal dates in the canon.

anchor_text: why wear you your leek to-day? Saint Davy's day is past.
summary: Saint David (Dewi Sant) is the patron saint of Wales, and his feast day, 1 March, is the occasion when Welsh people traditionally wear a leek in their hats as a badge of national pride. The scene is set after the battle and the peace negotiations — clearly past 1 March — so Gower is puzzled that Fluellen is still wearing his leek. Fluellen's answer explains the personal grievance: Pistol mocked him for the custom, and he is wearing the leek as a visible challenge until he can settle accounts.
detail: The leek's origin as a Welsh symbol is debated: one tradition held that Cadwallader (the seventh-century Welsh king) ordered his soldiers to wear leeks to distinguish themselves from the Saxons in battle; another pointed to a battle fought in a field of leeks. By Shakespeare's time the custom was well established enough to be a recognised national emblem, gently comic to an English audience. The scene turns the comic national badge into an instrument of honour and physical revenge.

anchor_text: art thou bedlam? Dost thou thirst, base Troyan
summary: 'Bedlam' is a shortened form of Bethlehem Royal Hospital in London, England's first asylum for the mentally ill, whose name became slang for madness itself. Pistol uses it as an insult: 'Are you out of your mind?' The word 'Troyan' (Trojan) was an Elizabethan slang term for a rogue, a dissolute fellow, or a low companion — used here as an insult but carrying the irony that Pistol himself is the swaggering blowhard.
detail: Bethlehem Royal Hospital (founded 1247, housing the mentally ill by the fourteenth century) was a well-known London landmark; its patients ('Bedlam beggars' or 'Toms o' Bedlam') wandered the streets begging. Pistol's rhetoric, with its rant-and-bluster register, is itself theatrical: he speaks in fragments of old bombast and insult. 'Troyan' as slang appears in 2 Henry IV and Merry Wives; it may glance at the tradition that the English were descended from Trojans via Brutus, making it a name the Welsh Fluellen might ironically own.

anchor_text: Not for Cadwallader and all his goats.
summary: Cadwallader (Welsh: Cadwaladr ap Cadwallon) was a seventh-century Welsh king, the last to claim sovereignty over all Britain. He became a figure of national legend and prophecy — Welsh tradition held that he would one day return to restore the British kingdom. Pistol's line mocks Welsh national pride by pairing the great legendary king with the cliché of Wales as a land of goats, meaning 'I will not do this even for the greatest Welsh hero and all his followers.'
detail: Cadwallader's prophecy of return (like Arthur's) was taken seriously enough that the Tudor dynasty, which was Welsh in origin, traded on it: Henry Tudor, Henry VII, was promoted as the fulfilment of the old British prophecy. Fluellen's passionate Welshness is part of the play's four-nations scheme (Welsh, Scottish, Irish, English captains in Henry's army, all under one king). Pistol's gibe — lumping Cadwallader with 'goats' (a standard slur against Wales) — is exactly the kind of mockery of Welsh national identity that provokes Fluellen to beat him.

The identification of Cadwallader as the last legendary British king and the Tudor dynasty's use of the Cadwallader prophecy are well-established; the gloss accurately explains why Pistol's pairing of Cadwallader with 'goats' is a deliberate mockery of Welsh national pride.

anchor_text: yesterday mountain-squire; but I will make you to-day a squire of low degree
summary: Fluellen turns Pistol's earlier insult into a pun. Pistol had called him a 'mountain-squire' — a contemptuous joke on Wales as a land of bare mountains, implying Fluellen is a low-born provincial nobody. Fluellen counters that he will make Pistol a 'squire of low degree' — that is, he will beat him down to ground level ('low degree' meaning both low social standing and physically low, knocked flat on the ground).
detail: 'Squire of low degree' plays on a popular medieval romance of that title, where a knight of humble origin proves his worth. Fluellen's wit is that 'low' collapses two meanings: the social humiliation Pistol wanted to inflict on him is reversed and applied to Pistol's own body, beaten down by the cudgel. The joke works because Fluellen, pedantic and precise in speech, turns Pistol's bragging insult back with scholarly tidiness.

anchor_text: good for your green wound and your ploody coxcomb
summary: A 'coxcomb' is a fool's cap — the cap with a cockscomb (rooster's crest) worn by a court jester — and by extension it meant the head itself, often in the sense of a fool's head. The jester's coxcomb-cap was a familiar stage prop, and calling a man's head his 'coxcomb' was to call him a fool at the same time. Fluellen's word 'ploody' (bloody) is the stereotyped Welsh pronunciation of 'bl-' as 'pl-', part of Shakespeare's comic rendering of Fluellen's accent throughout.

anchor_text: Doth Fortune play the huswife with me now?
summary: Fortune here is the classical goddess of luck and fate, imagined as a 'huswife' (housewife) — but in Elizabethan slang 'huswife' also meant a hussy or a woman of loose character (the same word as 'hussy'). So Pistol asks: Is Fortune playing the slut with me now, cheating and debasing me? It is a compressed version of the traditional image of Fortune as an unreliable, fickle woman who gives and snatches away.
detail: The classical image of Fortune as a fickle woman — turning her wheel to raise the low and cast down the high — runs through the play. Pistol's compressed joke collapses 'housewife' and 'hussy' in one: Fortune is both the homely woman who manages your affairs and the faithless woman who mismanages them for sport. The same double meaning appears in the Player's prayer in Hamlet (2.2) calling Fortune a 'strumpet' (prostitute). Pistol's speech begins a soliloquy of defeat: his bombast crumbles into the reality that his wife is dead, his friends hanged, and he faces England penniless.

anchor_text: my Doll is dead i' the spital Of malady of France
summary: A 'spital' (short for 'hospital') was one of London's charitable institutions for the sick and destitute. The 'malady of France' was a common Elizabethan term for syphilis — also called the French pox, the French disease, or the Neapolitan disease, each nation blaming another for its origin. Pistol learns that Doll Tearsheet, his companion from the Eastcheap tavern world, has died in a venereal disease ward.
detail: Syphilis reached Europe in the 1490s and spread rapidly; it was sometimes called 'morbus Gallicus' (the French disease) in Latin medical texts, which translates directly as 'malady of France.' Hospitals in London such as the Spital in Bishopsgate (St. Bartholomew's was another) took in the diseased poor. The information closes the circle on the Eastcheap world: Bardolph hanged, Nym hanged, the Boy killed at Agincourt, Mistress Quickly dead before the play began, and now Doll. Pistol is the last survivor of Falstaff's band, stripped of everything.

anchor_text: fatal balls of murdering basilisks
summary: A basilisk was a legendary serpent whose gaze or breath was said to kill instantly. Queen Isabel says Henry's eyes, once aimed at France like the lethal gaze of a basilisk, have now come in peace. 'Balls' here means eyeballs.
detail: The basilisk (also called the cockatrice) appears in Pliny's Natural History 8.33 and was a staple of Tudor bestiaries: a king of serpents whose look turned men to stone or whose breath killed at a distance. Shakespeare uses the creature elsewhere for lethal eyes (Richard III 1.2, 3 Henry VI 3.2). 'Fatal balls of murdering basilisks' packs three killing ideas together: 'fatal' = death-dealing, 'balls' = eyeballs, 'murdering basilisks' = the beast itself. The line is Isabel's diplomatic compliment in reverse: she acknowledges Henry's eyes were once weapons, and hopes they are now safe.

anchor_text: naked, poor, and mangled Peace, Dear nurse of arts
summary: Burgundy personifies Peace as a woman who has been stripped bare, impoverished, and wounded by years of war. 'Nurse of arts' means that peace is what makes learning, culture, and prosperity possible. This is the opening of a sustained speech comparing war-ravaged France to an untended garden.
detail: The personification of Peace (Latin Pax) as a goddess or woman extends through the whole speech. The coupling 'nurse of arts, plenties, and joyful births' recalls the classical topos of the Golden Age under peace — a commonplace from Virgil's Eclogues and the pacifist strain of Erasmus's influential Complaint of Peace (Querela Pacis, 1517). Burgundy was the historical broker of the Treaty of Troyes (1420) that ended the war; the speech reflects his role. 'Mangled' anticipates the imagery of wounded bodies and overgrown fields that follows.

anchor_text: fallow leas The darnel, hemlock, and rank fumitory, Doth root upon
summary: 'Fallow leas' are fields left unploughed and idle. Darnel, hemlock, and fumitory are weeds that take over neglected farmland: darnel is a rye-grass that can contaminate grain, hemlock a poisonous plant, fumitory a bitter-leaved weed. Burgundy is saying the war has let France's farmland go to worthless, even dangerous, plants.
detail: 'Fallow' means ploughed but left unsown, or simply unworked; 'leas' are meadows or arable fields (OED s.v. 'lea'). Darnel (Lolium temulentum) could cause dizziness and was hard to tell from wheat until it seeded — medieval grain laws tried to keep it out of harvests. Hemlock (Conium maculatum) is lethally poisonous. Fumitory (Fumaria officinalis) was medicinal but also a common weed of disturbed soil. The trio signals a landscape not merely idle but actively corrupted.

anchor_text: coulter rusts That should deracinate such savagery
summary: A 'coulter' is the iron blade at the front of a plough that cuts vertically through the soil ahead of the main ploughshare. 'Deracinate' means to uproot by the roots. Burgundy is saying the plough-blade, which should tear these weeds out, lies rusting unused because war has driven the farmers away.
detail: 'Coulter' from Latin culter (knife); OED records the form from Old English. 'Deracinate' is one of the relatively rare Latinate verbs Shakespeare coins or favours; from French déraciner, 'to uproot' (racine = root). It appears also in Troilus and Cressida 1.3. The image of rusting agricultural tools as a sign of civilisational collapse was a humanist commonplace, indebted to Virgil's Georgics on the ruin of farmland in civil war.

anchor_text: even mead, that erst brought sweetly forth The freckled cowslip, burnet, and green clover
summary: 'Even mead' is a flat, level meadow. 'Erst' means formerly, once upon a time. Cowslip and burnet are wild flowers of English meadows; 'kexes' (line 2787) are the dry hollow stalks of dead plants such as cow-parsley or hemlock. The catalogue contrasts what the meadow once grew with what it now produces.
detail: 'Mead' (Old English mæd) = meadow. 'Erst' from OE ærest = formerly; archaic by Shakespeare's time and consciously literary. Cowslip (Primula veris) is a common English spring flower; burnet (Sanguisorba minor) a low-growing herb of chalk grassland. 'Kexes' are the dead, hollow, rattling stems of umbellifers (cow-parsley, hemlock) left standing in winter fields. The movement from living flower to dry stalk enacts the metaphor: war starves the land of tending.

anchor_text: Whose tenours and particular effects You have enschedul'd briefly in your hands

anchor_text: plain king that thou wouldst think I had sold my farm to buy my crown
summary: Henry jokes that he is so bluntly ordinary that Katharine would think he had bought his crown cheaply, like a farmer who sells his land for ready cash. It is self-deprecating humour designed to disarm her: he is claiming he is no silky courtier, just an honest plain man.

anchor_text: sit like a jack-an-apes, never off
summary: A 'jack-an-apes' (also 'jackanapes') was a tame monkey — a popular pet in Tudor England, often kept on a chain. The phrase 'gasp out my eloquence' extends the image: the stuttering, breathless suitor. Henry boasts of the opposite — blunt, sworn honesty.

anchor_text: Je quand sur le possession de France, et quand vous avez le possession de moi
summary: Henry attempts French but produces mangled grammar: roughly 'I when upon the possession of France, and when you have the possession of me... Saint Denis be my speed! ... therefore yours is France and you are mine.' The joke is that his French is as broken as Katharine's English. A correct translation: 'When I am in possession of France, and when you have possession of me, then yours is France and you are mine.'

anchor_text: Je te prie, m'enseignez; il faut que j'apprenne a parler

anchor_text: sprays of us, The emptying of our fathers' luxury, Our scions put in wild and savage stock, Spirt up so suddenly into the clouds, And overlook their grafters
summary: The Dauphin uses the language of horticulture to sneer at the English. 'Sprays' are small shoots or twigs; 'scions' are young offshoots grafted onto older rootstock; 'grafters' are those who do the grafting — by extension, the French stock that produced the English graft. He is saying: we French are the ancient stock, the English are merely wild, inferior shoots taken from us — yet those shoots are now outgrowing us. The insult is aimed at the Normans who colonized England: the English are France's own degenerate offshoots.
detail: The Dauphin's metaphor plays on the Norman Conquest of 1066, when French-speaking Normans became England's ruling class. He implies that the English are literally made of French ancestry ('the emptying of our fathers' luxury' means the surplus or profligate children of French fathers, scattered like seed), but they have 'gone native,' grafted onto 'wild and savage stock.' The paradox he cannot explain is why these degenerate scions now 'overlook their grafters,' i.e. rise above and look down on the French who bred them. It is self-contempt disguised as contempt for England. Bourbon's next line, 'Normans, but bastard Normans, Norman bastards,' picks up the same idea.

anchor_text: teach lavoltas high, and swift corantos; Saying our grace is only in our heels, And that we are most lofty runaways
summary: Bourbon says French noblewomen are mocking them by suggesting they should go to English dancing schools to learn 'lavoltas' and 'corantos' — two fashionable court dances — since the French show spirit only in their heels, i.e. by running away. A lavolta was a dance with high leaps; a coranto was a fast, running dance. The gibe is that the French are fit only for leaping and sprinting — as they do when they flee.
detail: The lavolta (Italian 'la volta,' the turn) was a vigorous partnered dance in which the man lifted the woman high into the air, fashionable in the 1580s-90s and performed at Elizabeth I's court. The coranto (French courante, a running dance) was quick and gliding. Both required agile, springy use of the legs. The noblewomen's gibe collapses two meanings: 'our grace is only in our heels' means both 'we are elegant only at dancing' and 'we show our quality only by running away.' 'Lofty runaways' completes the pun — the high leaps of the lavolta and the high speed of flight are the same motion.

anchor_text: let not Bardolph's vital thread be cut With edge of penny cord
summary: Pistol's florid language here piles two images on top of each other: 'vital thread' alludes to the three Fates of Greek myth, who spun, measured, and cut the thread of every human life at death, while 'penny cord' is plain English for the cheap hangman's rope. Pistol wraps a mundane execution ('penny cord,' a rope that costs a penny) in classical-epic diction to make the plea sound grander than it is. A 'windpipe suffocate' (1411) with 'hemp' works the same way: strangled by rope, in grand words. All this oratory fails: Fluellen refuses to intercede.

anchor_text: Ill will never said well
summary: Orleans and the Constable trade proverbs in a contest of wit — 'Ill will never said well,' 'There is flattery in friendship,' 'Give the devil his due,' 'A pox of the devil,' and 'A fool's bolt is soon shot.' Each proverb is deployed as a weapon in their sparring, and each is capped or deflected by the next. The exchange is a verbal duel that mirrors the battle to come.
detail: The practice of 'capping proverbs' — trumping an opponent's saying with a better or contradictory one — was a recognized form of Elizabethan wit-play, taught in rhetoric manuals as argument by commonplace (sententia). 'A fool's bolt is soon shot' means a fool fires off his arrow quickly and is then defenceless; 'You have shot over' (you overshot the mark) lets the Constable turn it back on Orleans. 'Give the devil his due' (credit even an enemy) and 'A pox of the devil' escalate the wordplay into mock-cursing. The exchange reveals the French lords' complacency the night before a battle they expect to win easily.

anchor_text: Sweats in the eye of Phoebus, and all night Sleeps in Elysium; next day after dawn, Doth rise and help Hyperion to his horse
summary: Phoebus (a title of Apollo) and Hyperion were both names for the sun-god, imagined as driving a chariot of fiery horses across the sky each day. 'Sweating in the eye of Phoebus' means working all day in the blazing sun. At day's end the sun-god must be helped back onto his horse for the next morning — the slave's daily labour mirrors the cosmic cycle. Henry's point is that the slave, who sweats in the sun all day and sleeps in bliss all night, has a more enviable existence than a king who cannot sleep; the cosmic scale of the imagery makes the king's insomnia seem cosmic too.

anchor_text: the tucket sonance and the note to mount
summary: A 'tucket' was a personal trumpet fanfare sounded to identify a nobleman — the Elizabethan equivalent of a call-sign. 'Sonance' simply means the sound or sounding of it. Heralds and trumpeters each carried set calls, and the specific sequence the Constable names — tucket first, then the mount signal — is recognizable military ceremony to an Elizabethan audience.

anchor_text: Big Mars seems bankrupt in their beggar'd host, And faintly through a rusty beaver peeps

anchor_text: The man that once did sell the lion's skin While the beast liv'd, was kill'd with hunting him
summary: Henry is alluding to a fable from the Aesopic tradition: a hunter sold a lion's (in some versions a bear's) skin before he had caught the animal, then was killed in the hunt. anchor_text: O diable! O Seigneur! le jour est perdu, tout est perdu

anchor_text: fold up Parca's fatal web
summary: Parca (plural Parcae) was the Roman name for the Fates — three goddesses who spun, measured, and cut the thread of every mortal's life. Pistol threatens Fluellen with death in grandiose, theatrical terms: to 'fold up' the Fates' 'fatal web' is to wind up and end the fabric of a life.

Pistol's inflated classical allusion is comic because it borrows old bombastic stage-rhetoric and applies it to the petty situation of being asked to eat a leek.

anchor_text: 'a babbled of green fields
summary: This phrase does not appear in the 1600 Quarto or the 1623 Folio. The Folio reads 'a Table of greene fields,' which most editors from Lewis Theobald (1726) onward have emended to 'a babbled of green fields,' arguing that 'Table' is a compositor's misreading of an old-style script 'b' as 'T.' The emendation is now standard but remains a conjecture, not a reading from any authoritative text.
detail: Theobald first proposed the reading in his 1726 book Shakespeare Restored: a secretary-hand 'babbled' was, he argued, misread by the Folio compositor as 'a Table.' The phrase, once accepted, became one of the most celebrated in Shakespeare: a dying man murmuring of Psalm 23 ('He maketh me to lie down in green pastures') is emotionally apt for Falstaff, who in life was associated with taverns, sack, and waste — and who at death, in Quickly's account, seems to reach toward something pastoral and innocent. Editors who defend the Folio ('a table of green fields') take it as a geographic note or a lost allusion, but the majority follow Theobald. The phrase is marked medium-confidence because it rests entirely on emendation; readers should know they are responding to a brilliant eighteenth-century guess, not a word Shakespeare demonstrably wrote.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 955

Rescued in 2026-06-01 review sweep — Generalized the Ovid citation from the wrong precise locus (2.401-2, which is the Callisto episode) to Book 2, where Jove does wield the thunderbolt against Phaethon; the interpretation that the thunderbolt is the emblem of irresistible sovereignty was verified.

Jupiter's thunderbolt as the emblem of irresistible sovereign compulsion is a commonplace of Roman poetry and the comparison is explicitly in the text; the Ovid Met. 2 citation is to the Phaethon episode where the thunderbolt is wielded, which is a legitimate though not unique locus for this image.
